# 1. R and RStudio

## R and RStudio are two different programs

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**R**

The programming language and the engine that runs your code.

It does the computing.
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**RStudio**

An IDE: editor, plot pane, help viewer, file browser.

It does no computing itself. It hands your code to R.
:::
:::

**Install R first, RStudio second.**

Once installed, you open **RStudio**, not R.

## Installing R

<https://cran.r-project.org/>

**Windows**

*Download R for Windows* → *base* → the big link at the top. Accept every default.

**macOS**

*Download R for macOS* → the **arm64** `.pkg` for Apple silicon (M1 to M4), the
**x86_64** `.pkg` for older Intel Macs. Accept every default.

::: {.notes}
Apple menu, About This Mac, tells them which chip they have.
:::

## Installing RStudio

<https://posit.co/download/rstudio-desktop/>

**RStudio Desktop**, the free version. Install with the defaults.

## Exercise 1: get R running {background-color="#f0f4f8"}

1. Install R
2. Install RStudio
3. Open RStudio, click into the Console, type:

```{r eval=FALSE}
R.version.string
```

You should see `"R version 4.4.1 ..."`. Any version 4 is fine.

**If anything fails, raise your hand.**

## Installation problems and how to fix them

| Problem | Fix |
|--------------------------|--------------------------------------|
| RStudio cannot find R | You installed only RStudio. Install R, then restart |
| "R session failed to start" | Restart. Then `Tools > Global Options > General`, point *R version* at your installation |
| macOS: "developer cannot be verified" | Right-click the file, *Open*. Or `System Settings > Privacy & Security > Open Anyway` |
| Windows user name with a space or accent | R struggles with the library path. Come and see me |
| No admin rights | Install "for this user only" |

# 2. The RStudio window

## RStudio has four panes

![](figures/rstudio_panes.png){width=85% fig-align="center"}

## Source is for scripts, Console is where code runs

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Source**, top left

Where you write and save scripts.

Nothing here runs on its own.

`Ctrl+Enter` sends a line to R.
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Console**, bottom left

Where code runs and output appears.

Nothing typed here is saved.
:::
:::

**Environment**, top right: the objects in memory.

**Files / Plots / Packages / Help**, bottom right.

## `>` means R is ready, `+` means your command is unfinished

`>` R is waiting for a command. Normal.

`+` R thinks your command is unfinished, usually an open bracket or quotation mark.

Press `Esc` to cancel the line and type it again.

::: {.notes}
This is the moment beginners think R has frozen. Show it live: type sqrt(16 and Enter.
:::

## R as a calculator

```{r}
2 + 2
20 / 8
2^3
sqrt(16)
round(3.14159, 2)
```

## Arithmetic operators

| Operator | Meaning | Example | Result |
|----|-----------------|-----------|------|
| `+` | addition | `7 + 3` | 10 |
| `-` | subtraction | `7 - 3` | 4 |
| `*` | multiplication | `7 * 3` | 21 |
| `/` | division | `7 / 3` | 2.333 |
| `^` | power | `7^2` | 49 |
| `%%` | remainder | `7 %% 3` | 1 |

Anything after `#` is a comment. R ignores it.

## An error stops R, a warning does not

```{r error=TRUE}
sqrt("four")
```

R tells you what is wrong: `sqrt()` needs numbers, you gave it text.

An **error** means R stopped and did nothing.

A **warning** means R did something and wants you to know it was odd:

```{r warning=TRUE}
sqrt(-1)
```

## `?` opens the help page for any command

```{r eval=FALSE}
?round      # the help page for round()
??regression   # search the documentation
```

Start with the **Examples** at the bottom of the page. Copy them into the Console and
run them.

# 3. Folders, paths and the working directory

## Most file errors mean R is looking in the wrong folder

`cannot open file` almost always means R was looking in the wrong folder.

A **directory** is a folder. Directories form a tree:

```
Documents
  2026_Data_Handling
    course
    exercises
      data
        swiss.csv
      code
        hello_world.R
```

## Absolute and relative paths

A **path** is the address of a file or a folder.

**Absolute**, starts at the top of your disk:

```
C:/Users/anna/Documents/2026_Data_Handling/exercises/data/swiss.csv     (Windows)
/Users/anna/Documents/2026_Data_Handling/exercises/data/swiss.csv       (Mac)
```

**Relative**, starts from where you are now:

```
exercises/data/swiss.csv     swiss.csv, in the folder data, inside exercises
../swiss.csv                 swiss.csv, one folder up
```

Absolute paths break as soon as the folder moves. **Use relative paths.**

## The working directory is where R looks

Where R currently is. Every relative path is read from it.

```{r eval=FALSE}
getwd()       # which folder am I in?
list.files()  # what is in it?
```

Run both whenever R says a file does not exist.

On Windows, write paths with **forward slashes**: `C:/Users/...`

A single backslash has a special meaning in R and will cause errors.

## An RStudio Project sets the working directory for you

A folder with a small `.Rproj` file in it.

Open the project and RStudio sets the working directory to that folder automatically,
on any computer.

Your relative paths always work, and you never need `setwd()`.

# 4. Scripts

## Use the Console to try things, a script to keep them

Everything you type in the Console disappears when you close RStudio.

A **script** is a plain text file, ending in `.R`, that holds your code so you can save
it, correct it and run it again.

- `Ctrl+Enter` (`Cmd+Enter`) runs the current line or the selection
- the **Run** button does the same
- `source("exercises/code/my_script.R")` runs a whole script from the Console

Writing a line in the Source pane does nothing until you send it to R.

## Exercise 4: your first script {background-color="#f0f4f8"}

1. In the Console: `print("Hello world")`
2. `File > New File > R Script`
3. Type `print("Hello world")` on the first line
4. `Ctrl+Enter` to run it
5. Save it into `exercises/code` as `hello_world.R`
6. In the Console:

```{r eval=FALSE}
source("exercises/code/hello_world.R")
```

The path in step 6 is relative, and it works because the project set your working
directory.

# 5. Objects, and the arrow `<-`

## Save a result with the arrow `<-`

```{r}
x <- 5
```

Read it as "x gets 5". Nothing prints: R stored the value instead of showing it.

`x` now appears in the **Environment** pane.

```{r}
x
```

## Objects can be used to build other objects

```{r}
y <- 3
z <- x + y
z
```

`z` was computed once. Changing `x` afterwards does not update `z`:

```{r}
x <- 100
z
```

No live link between objects, unlike a spreadsheet.

## Four rules for naming objects

- **R overwrites without warning.** `x <- 100` silently replaced the 5
- **Names are case sensitive.** `data`, `Data`, `DATA` are three objects
- **Names start with a letter**, no spaces, no accents. `income_2023`, not `2023_income`
- **Use `<-`, not `=`.** Shortcut: `Alt+-` (`Option+-` on Mac)

```{r eval=FALSE}
ls()              # what is in memory
rm(list = ls())   # clear it
```

# 6. Packages

## A package is a set of commands written by other people

Collections of commands written by other people, published on CRAN.

Over 20,000 of them. In this course:

| Package | For |
|-----------|--------------------------------------|
| `dplyr` | handling data |
| `ggplot2` | graphics |
| `readxl` | reading Excel files |

## `install.packages()` once, `library()` every session

```{r eval=FALSE}
install.packages("dplyr")   # ONCE per computer
library(dplyr)              # EVERY time you open R
```

`install.packages()` downloads the package and copies it onto your hard disk.
Quotation marks around the name.

`library()` makes an installed package available in this session.
No quotation marks.

**Install once, load every session.**

## Common package error messages

| Message | Meaning |
|---------------------------------|--------------------------------|
| `there is no package called 'dplyr'` | Not installed. `install.packages("dplyr")` |
| `could not find function "filter"` | Installed but not loaded. `library(dplyr)` |
| `built under R version ...` | A warning, not an error. Usually harmless |

If R asks about installing *from sources*, answer `n`.

The *masked from package:stats* message is information, not an error.

## Exercise 6: packages {background-color="#f0f4f8"}

```{r eval=FALSE}
install.packages(c("dplyr", "ggplot2", "readxl"))

library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(readxl)
```

3. In the Packages tab, bottom right, find `dplyr`. Is it ticked?
4. Restart R with `Ctrl+Shift+F10`, then run `ggplot()`.
   What happens, and what do you have to do about it?

# 7. Quarto

## A Quarto document mixes text and runnable code

The `.qmd` files in the course repository, including your handout, are **Quarto**
documents: normal writing plus executable R code chunks.

Rendering runs the code and drops the results, tables and plots straight into the
finished PDF or HTML.

Nothing is copied by hand from R into Word, so the table and the data cannot disagree.

Try it: `File > New File > Quarto Document...`, accept the defaults, click **Render**.

# Self-study: vectors

## A vector holds several values at once

We come back to vectors in week 3. Read this at home if you want a head start.

Several values in one object, built with `c()` for "combine":

```{r}
income <- c(52000, 48000, 61000, 55000, 49000)
income
```

Text goes in quotation marks:

```{r}
canton <- c("SG", "ZH", "BE", "SG", "VD")
length(income)
mean(income)
```

A column of a data set is exactly this.
